“But realize this, that in the last days difficult times will be present.

For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, having been puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. And turn away from these.” - 2 Timothy 3:1-5 (BLB)

A culture can keep the costume after the body is gone.

The words stay. The aesthetics stay. The platforms, the outrage, the Bible references, the moral confidence, the branding — all of it can stay standing long after the thing inside it has died. Paul saw this coming, and what he wrote is worse than a warning about atheism. Open godlessness you can spot from across the room. This is harder to see, because Paul’s list doesn’t end in rebellion.

It ends in religion.

2 Timothy 3:1-5 — Paul is writing to Timothy about the last days, and the sins he names run in a specific order: lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, savage, haters of good, traitors, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God — and then, last on the list, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Paul’s instruction to Timothy is blunt: turn away from these.

Form of godliness.

Outward shape without inward life. The husk still stands. The appearance still passes at a distance. But the power inside it has been refused, and refused is not the same word as lost. Paul isn’t describing a slow fade. He’s describing a decision.

This doesn’t mean every church is dead, or every ministry corrupt, or every public work of faith suspect on sight. That’s not discernment. That’s just pride. Paul isn’t handing the reader a license to stand outside the church and sneer at it.

He’s putting the reader under the same exam.

Because the danger was never only that they might keep the costume while gutting what’s underneath it. The danger is that we learn to look alive too.

The Order Is the Argument

Paul isn’t dumping sins into a bag at random. Read the list again and there’s an order to the rot: it opens with disordered love and closes with religious form. Self-love is the root. Pleasure-love is where the root leads. The form of godliness is the leaf cover that makes the dead branch look like it’s still in the orchard.

A man can say God first while self sits on the throne the whole time. A man can preach against materialism while money is quietly running the calendar. A man can defend truth with a mouth that slanders anyone who disagrees with him. A man can call for holiness in public and hold no discipline in private. A man can build an entire platform on Christian language while being formed, underneath it, by the exact appetites he built the platform to condemn.

Godliness doesn’t usually vanish outright. It goes hollow first. A shape kept standing with nothing left inside it to hold the shape up.

Self-Love, Money-Love, and the Persona

Paul opens with lovers of self, not confidence, not a personality trait, but the self enthroned as center of gravity. Once that happens, truth only gets used when it flatters the image. Community only matters when it affirms. Correction gets recast as abuse. A man that hungry can turn even his own repentance into content.

The costume stays Christian. The center does not stay Christ.

Lovers of money comes right behind it, and the issue was never that ministry needs funding, ministry has always needed funding. The issue is gain working as a hidden discipler, shaping what gets said and what gets softened before the speaker even notices the edit happening. It rarely announces itself as greed. It calls itself impact. It calls itself scale. Sometimes those words are honest. Sometimes they’re cologne on ambition

Boasting and arrogance follow naturally once self is centered and gain is loved, the persona becomes the thing being protected. Arrogance doesn’t always sound like I’m above everyone. Often it sounds like no one else is brave enough to say what I’m saying, or the criticism just proves I’m over the target. That’s how truth-telling gets worn as a costume for pride, and Paul already closed that particular exit:

1 Corinthians 13:1-3 — a man can speak in every tongue, hold every mystery, carry faith that moves mountains, give away everything he owns, hand over his own body, and without love, Paul calls the whole performance nothing. Not diminished. Nothing.

Gift without love isn’t maturity. Volume without love isn’t courage. A file full of citations without love isn’t a prophetic office. It’s noise, dressed in Scripture.

The Power Being Denied

Worth defining, because this is the spot where people smuggle in their favorite argument. Paul isn’t reducing “the power of godliness” to miracles or spiritual fireworks, the New Testament has no embarrassment about the supernatural. What’s being denied here is narrower and harder to fake: the power that actually makes a man godly. Repentance. Obedience. Self-control. Holiness. Endurance. Humility. Freedom from the very loves Paul just listed off.

Galatians lays the same ground from the other direction:

Galatians 5:22-23 — the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Against these, Paul says, there is no law.

Set that next to the 2 Timothy list and the contrast is brutal. Self-love against love. Money-love against goodness. Boasting against gentleness. Run the two lists side by side.

It’s a different root entirely. The Spirit doesn’t touch up the shell, He replaces what’s growing underneath it.

The Modern Version Has Better Lighting

None of this is an argument against beauty, art, production value, or a platform that actually reaches people. A church isn’t holier for having a broken microphone. Bad sound isn’t a spiritual fruit.

The failure point is more specific than aesthetics. It’s the form surviving after the power inside it has been cut off at the root: Christian branding with no repentance behind it. Christian content built for self-promotion wearing a ministry label. Christian outrage running with no holiness underneath it to justify the anger. Platform-building with no private obedience backing it up. Christian language rented out to baptize ordinary ambition. “Truth-telling” that’s really content farming, wearing boldness as a costume for the love it doesn’t have.

None of that is visibility, or excellence, or growth. Those aren’t the problem, KC exists to grow. The counterfeit is when the Christian shape gets kept for what it’s useful for, profitable, tribal, familiar, impressive, while the power that actually transforms a man gets quietly shown the door.

A man can build a platform defending biblical truth and still be owned by the same cravings Paul named two thousand years back. A church can have sound doctrine, sharp branding, and the right enemies named from the pulpit, and still have no pulse.

That’s 2 Timothy 3, running on better cameras.

Matthew 23: The Mirror Held to the Institution

Jesus already diagnosed this exact disease, and He diagnosed it in front of men who knew the forms cold, Scripture, public office, visible seriousness. Men who knew exactly how to look clean.

Matthew 23:27-28 — whitewashed tombs, Jesus calls them. Beautiful on the outside. Full of dead men’s bones on the inside. Righteous to the eye of anyone watching from the street. Full of lawlessness underneath the paint.

A whitewashed tomb isn’t ugly looking. That’s the point, it’s been treated, cleaned, managed, dressed up for public viewing. The outside isn’t chaos. It’s polish. And Jesus isn’t fooled by polish, isn’t dazzled by institutional shine, isn’t softened by the right vocabulary when greed is sitting in the cup underneath it.

But don’t read this and go looking for pastors to point at. Matthew 23 isn’t a spectator sport for laymen who like watching leadership get cooked. It’s a mirror, and the same disease scales down to fit smaller rooms, a family’s reputation, a personal brand, a theology account, a marriage, a private fantasy of being seen as righteous. The tomb doesn’t need a megachurch budget behind it.

Whitewash is cheap. Anyone can afford a coat.

Sardis Had a Name

Revelation 3:1 — Christ writes to the church at Sardis and tells them plainly: you have a name, a reputation for being alive, and you are dead.

That line should sit uncomfortably in every ministry, platform, household, and soul that’s learned to run on reputation instead of life. Sardis wasn’t obscure. People had heard of it. That was the whole danger, the name was doing the work the life was supposed to be doing.

A church can carry a reputation with no pulse behind it. A man can be known for spiritual things while dying quietly behind the label. Put Matthew 7, 2 Timothy 3, and Revelation 3 next to each other: Matthew 7 shows men standing before Christ with their religious paperwork in hand. 2 Timothy 3 names the loves that make the paperwork look convincing. Revelation 3 tells a church, that a reputation cannot raise a corpse.

The World Wearing Church Clothes

Paul’s list here runs close to Romans 1 for a reason, men who trade the glory of God for disordered want, corrupted thinking, and moral collapse. Easy to read that as a passage about the world out there. Harder to see how often the world’s loves get smuggled into church buildings wearing a cross on the lapel.

John warns against loving the world. James calls friendship with the world enmity against God. Philippians names men whose god is their belly and whose minds never leave the ground. None of that is a script for feeling superior to unbelievers. It’s a warning to God’s own people against baptizing the world’s appetites and calling the water ministry.

The world was never going to need the church to renounce Christ out loud. It only needed the church to keep His name on the sign while it adopted the world’s hunger underneath it. Keep the vocabulary. Keep the worship set. Keep the approved enemies. Keep the public prayers, the content calendar, the whole apparatus running.

Just let go of the power that crucifies self, disciplines desire, forgives the man who wronged you, and holds a man obedient when nobody with a camera is watching.

A costume can carry a corpse a long way down the road before anyone checks the pulse.

The Audit Is Love

First Corinthians 13 belongs in this field because it cuts down one of religion’s favorite hiding places: a crop of visible spiritual intensity with no fruit of love: tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, radical generosity, even the body handed over in sacrifice, Paul stacks up every impressive category available to a man and then tells him plainly that without love, the total comes to nothing.

That’s not a knock against doctrine, and it’s not sentimental mush set to a worship track. Biblical love doesn’t flinch from the truth, it rejoices in it. But Paul refuses to let performance pass as maturity, and that’s the test that actually matters for a culture strong on production and thin on love: are the people coming out the other side patient, kind, faithful under pressure? Or suspicious, loud, tribal, entertained by their own outrage?

Love Is Not the Word You Think It Is

Most modern ears hear love and translate it to nice. Harmless. Agreeable. Never the one to raise his voice.

That’s not the word Paul used.

1 Corinthians 13:4-7 — patient, kind, doesn’t envy, doesn’t boast, isn’t puffed up, doesn’t act unbecomingly, doesn’t seek its own, isn’t provoked, doesn’t take account of wrong suffered, doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness but rejoices with the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Every verb in that list is something a man does. None of them is a feeling he privately holds while staying silent.

Rejoicing with the truth is on that list. Silence isn’t. Agreement isn’t. Comfort isn’t.

Proverbs already priced this out: faithful are the wounds of a friend, meaning a wound from someone who loves you costs less than a kiss from someone flattering you toward the grave. Paul tells the Ephesians to speak the truth in love, which only makes sense as a command if speaking the truth and loving someone were ever in tension to begin with. Love was never the absence of confrontation. It’s what makes the confrontation cost the speaker something instead of costing him nothing.

A culture that’s redefined love as never offend hasn’t gotten kinder. It’s gotten a counterfeit that lets it call cowardice a virtue.

Avoid Such People

Paul closes the warning with an order: avoid them. That’s not a license for paranoia, not a call to treat every struggling believer as radioactive, the church has always been a hospital. But there’s a real line between weakness under repentance and rebellion wearing religious form, between a man who hates his own sin and a performer protecting his. Paul is telling Timothy that certain people, certain whole cultures, are dangerous precisely because the form still holds, enough shape to pass inspection, enough vocabulary to blend into the room, enough confidence to recruit behind it.

Avoiding that isn’t snobbery. It’s how you stay alive. You don’t stay near a corpse and keep your health.

The Costume Cannot Stand Before Christ

A culture built on counterfeit godliness produces men fluent in Lord, Lord who love themselves, money, pleasure, status, and applause underneath the fluency. It produces men who can speak Christian without ever obeying Christ where no one’s watching. It produces men who’ve stopped telling the difference between reputation and life.

That’s why the secret place in Matthew 6 still matters more than the stage. The Father sees what the audience can’t. The audience sees the form. The Father sees whether there’s a root under it, or just a shape somebody’s still watering out of habit.

A culture can keep the form of godliness running for a long time on reputation alone. But the form was never going to be able to save anybody. A costume cannot raise the dead.

And Christ was never going to confuse a name for a life.
